connector: The last chapter ended with a secret told after dark: Ellen will stay with the Johansens. Now it is the middle of the night, and someone is pounding on the door. Three officers are inside the apartment in seconds. Watch for the one thing Annemarie sees that the soldiers must not see, and what she does about it.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Grete. In this chapter, it’s the middle of the night, and someone is pounding on the Johansens’ door. Annemarie will have only seconds to decide what to do. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 5, and try saying one sentence three ways. Today’s question: what does courage look like when there’s no time to think?
transcripts.wgrd: This week’s reading move is about proof. It isn’t enough to say a character is brave. You have to point to the exact moment, the thing she does, and say what could have gone wrong. As you read, keep one finger ready. When Annemarie acts, mark the spot.
transcripts.dol: The model is short and plain. The sentence to fix has someone asking a question out loud, so it needs quotation marks and a question mark in the right places. Two sentences are squeezed together, too, and one describing word needs a small joining mark.
transcripts.guide1: This week’s word work starts with noticing again. Nobody tells you the rule first. In grammar, you’ll look at who is doing each action. In spelling, you’ll look for words that have been built from smaller parts. Find the pattern yourself, and it will stay with you.
transcripts.morphology: This week we leave the city for the sea. Two old roots do the work. One means to believe. The other means to stretch. Each stretching word reaches a beam of light across the water, and each believing word lights a window on the far shore. Read the meaning, then pick the root.
transcripts.vocabulary: Four new words follow you through Chapters 5 to 8. One is about planning, one about being believed, one about keeping quiet, and one about how your body feels when you’re afraid. Read each sentence, take the word apart if you can, and make a guess before you flip the card.
transcripts.grammar: Every action needs someone to do it. Read the sentence and find each little word that stands in for a person, then look at the verb right beside it. Some verbs have an extra ending and some don’t. What decides it? That’s the rule you’re here to find.
transcripts.spelling: Lots of long words are really short words wearing extra pieces: something added at the front, something added at the end, or both. Tap each word that’s been built this way. Then ask yourself: if I took the pieces off, what word would be left underneath?
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Courage Watch is about courage that has only seconds. When I was a girl, I saw a woman on a tram drop a paper she shouldn’t have had. Her friend stepped on it before anyone noticed, without a word. I’ve never forgotten how fast she moved. Watch Annemarie in this chapter. She doesn’t stop to think. She acts.
transcripts.read: This chapter is short, and most of it happens in the dark. Read slowly. Listen for sounds: boots, voices, doors. Notice what Annemarie sees that the soldiers must not see, and what Papa reaches for when the questions get dangerous. Stop at each pause question before you go on.
transcripts.copia: Here is one plain sentence about the necklace. Your job is to say it three new ways: a new beginning, a stronger verb, and a detail about where or how. The bones of the sentence stay the same. But each version makes a reader feel the moment a little differently.
transcripts.guide3: Now you write. Each question points at a small moment: what Annemarie does with her hands, what Papa does with the photographs, and what she finds in her palm afterward. Then, in your essay, you’ll learn to set a short quote inside your own sentence, so it fits smoothly.
transcripts.chapter: These questions ask you to look closely at small things: a chain, a photograph, a mark on a hand. Ask yourself why the author chose such tiny details for such a frightening night. Sometimes the smallest thing on the page is carrying the biggest feeling.
transcripts.workshop: Your essay starts to sound like real writing now. A quote dropped in by itself feels bumpy, like a stone in your shoe. Today you learn to give it a set-up before it and a so-what after it, so the reader knows exactly why it matters.

match.intend: Intend has the root that means stretch. Look for the meaning about planning to do something on purpose.
match.credible: Credible has the root that means believe. Look for the meaning about being easy to believe.
match.discreet: Discreet is about being careful and quiet. Look for the meaning about not drawing attention.
match.tense: Tense is a feeling in your body. Look for the meaning about being tight with worry.

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Each stretching word reaches the light across the water; each believing word lights a window on the far shore.

why.t: In Chapter 7, Annemarie stands on the shore at Gilleleje and points across the sea to Sweden. tend means to stretch, so each right tend word stretches the lighthouse beam a little farther across the water. cred means to believe, so each right cred word lights a window on the far shore. One stretch of water each lesson, until the light reaches Sweden.

notes.wgrd: When you say a character is brave, point to what she does, not just how she feels. Find the moment, name the risk, then say it in one line: she is brave because she…
vocab: To plan to do something on purpose.
notes.wordParts: cred means “to believe” (credible, incredible). tend means “to stretch” or “to reach” (extend, pretend, attend).
notes.grammar: A pronoun and its verb must agree. With he, she or it, the verb takes an s: she watches, he listens. With I, you, we or they, it doesn’t: they wait.
notes.spelling: Many long words are built from parts: a prefix in front (un-, re-, dis-), a base word, and a suffix at the end (-ful, -ly, -ness, -ance). Find the base underneath and keep its spelling: hope + ful + ly = hopefully.

plate.alt: A printed police notice with the large Danish word Mørklægning, meaning blackout.
plate.credit: A 1940 police notice ordering a blackout: at night every window in Denmark had to be covered so no light showed. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

case.title: A Star No Dane Had to Wear
case.alt: A yellow cloth star with six points and the German word Jude printed on it, shown on a dark background.
label: This yellow cloth star says Jude, the German word for Jew. In Germany and in many of the countries the Nazis ruled, Jewish people were forced to sew a star like this onto their coats, so that everyone could pick them out.

Denmark was different. The Danish government refused, and Danish Jews were never made to wear the yellow star. Ellen’s Star of David necklace in Chapter 5 is not a badge anyone forced on her. It is her own, and she wears it because she chooses to.

look.q: Why do you think the Nazis wanted Jewish people to wear a badge like this?
look.a: So they could be picked out in any crowd and treated differently. A badge took away a person’s chance to blend in.

look.q: Why was Ellen’s necklace so dangerous on the night the soldiers came?
look.a: The soldiers were hunting for Jewish families. A Star of David around her neck would have told them exactly who she was.

case.credit: A yellow badge (Judenstern) in the Jewish Museum Westphalia, Dorsten, Germany. Photo: Daniel Ullrich, Threedots, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
case.sub: A real object from the war years.
